---
title: Definitions
llms-description: "What a Steward definition is — any program culminating in a single eval_set() call — the three supported formats, how enumeration turns one into a manifest of resolved tasks, and the determinism the contract assumes."
---

## Overview

A **definition** is what says what your eval set contains. Steward's contract
for one is deliberately as wide as it can be:

> A definition is any program that culminates in a single `eval_set()` call.

That is not a format Steward invented. It is what people already write, which
is why Steward introduces no fourth format and asks you to migrate nothing. The
definition remains the single source of truth for what an eval set *is* —
Steward's own settings live elsewhere and are structurally barred from
contradicting it ([Standing Rules](directives.qmd)).

Three kinds of program satisfy the contract today:

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **`evalset.py`** | A plain Python file ending in `eval_set()`. The native mode. |
| **`flow.yaml`** | An [Inspect Flow](https://github.com/meridianlabs-ai/inspect_flow) spec, as YAML or Python. See [Inspect Flow](flow.qmd). |
| **`hawk.yaml`** | A [Hawk](https://github.com/METR/hawk) eval set config. See [Hawk](hawk.qmd). |

For the latter two, Steward runs *their* entrypoints rather than reimplementing
what they do, and intercepts at the `eval_set()` call. So Flow keeps its
includes, defaults merging, and hooks; Hawk keeps its task × solver × model
crossing, secrets resolution, and environment setup. Steward owns execution from
the boundary onward and nothing before it.

## How a definition is found

`steward init --type evalset|flow|hawk` places an empty placeholder, and the
type chooses its filename — nothing else. A workspace's definition is then
located **by name**:

``` text
evalset.py    flow.yaml    hawk.yaml
```

The name is a pointer, not a type declaration: what a definition *is* gets
decided by reading it, which happens later, when there is content to read. An
empty `.yaml` would validate as both a Flow spec and a Hawk config, so
filename-based lookup is what keeps an untouched workspace from reporting
itself ambiguous.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The definition's filename is fixed rather than configurable, and that is load
bearing for a reason nobody would look for. A task's identity includes the file
it was defined in, so renaming a definition gives every task in it a new
identity and orphans the entire previous run. A workspace with a fixed name has
nothing to rename.
:::

## Enumeration

Before anything runs, Steward needs the full list of tasks — so it can schedule
them, give each its own process, and know when they are done. It gets that by
**executing the definition** with interception enabled: at the `eval_set()`
call, tasks are resolved exactly as they normally would be, the resulting list
is written out, and the process exits before anything runs. Code after the
`eval_set()` call never executes, so result-processing side effects cannot fire
against empty results.

``` bash
steward tasks evalset.py
```

``` bash
steward tasks flow.yaml --json          # the full manifest
steward tasks flow.py -A model=gpt-5    # arguments for a Python flow spec
```

The result is a **manifest**: one row per resolved task, carrying its display
key, its stable identity, its dataset size, and its epochs. It is an *index
into* the definition rather than a replacement for it — which matters, because
of the next section.

`steward tasks` is a diagnostic and takes an explicit path. It is not part of
the normal workflow: [`steward launch`](running.qmd) captures the manifest
itself.

## Every process runs the whole definition

Definition files do real work when executed — `set_model_info()`, dynamically
constructed `Model` objects, environment mutation, dataset preparation. None of
that can be captured in a static artifact, so **every process that runs
evaluation work executes the definition itself**. A worker running one task
runs your whole file, then runs only its task.

Two consequences follow, and both are worth knowing:

-   Your definition runs identically by hand. `python evalset.py` is the same
    program; nothing in the file is Steward-specific.
-   Anything expensive that happens on the way to `eval_set()` happens once per
    worker. For a plain script that is imports. For Flow and Hawk it is more,
    which is what the [platform pages](flow.qmd) are largely about.

### The definition must be deterministic about its task list

Enumerate on Monday, run task 7 on Tuesday, and the selection has to still
match. So the contract assumes the definition produces the same task list on
every execution — no task construction that depends on the clock or on
randomness.

Drift is detected rather than papered over. A task Steward selected that
resolution fails to produce is a hard error naming it, and Steward hashes the
definition file so it can tell you the file changed after it was read. What that
hash covers is deliberately narrow — the top-level file and nothing else — and
its job is to prompt, not to guarantee. The safety net is the delta report on
the next [launch](amending.qmd), not the hash.

## What Steward will not accept

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **A second `eval_set()` call** | The contract is one call per definition. |
| **Dynamic task producers** | A `TaskSource` is fundamentally incompatible with enumerating tasks ahead of time, and enumeration fails with a clear error. |
| **Scanners, for now** | A definition declaring `scanner:` cannot be run by Steward yet. Enumeration records that it scans, so this is refused early rather than discovered when every worker fails. |

## Tasks and identity

The unit of work is a **resolved task** — a task × model × solver combination,
corresponding one-to-one with an eval log. A manifest of six rows becomes six
worker processes and six `.eval` files.

Two identities travel with each:

-   **A stable identifier**, which is Inspect's own. It hashes the task file and
    name, the arguments, the model, the resolved solver, the generate config,
    and the execution limits — so two tasks that differ only in temperature are
    correctly different tasks. This is what Steward matches logs against, and it
    is the reason a completed task is never re-run.
-   **A display key**, which is what you read: `mbpp[react]@openai/gpt-5`.
    Where several tasks would collide, the key gains only what distinguishes
    them — a differing argument, then a differing model argument, then an
    ordinal.

### Setting `max_samples` explicitly

Worth calling out because it is easy to leave off and expensive to leave off:

``` python
eval_set(..., max_samples=40)
```

Leaving it unset hands sample concurrency to the model's adaptive connection
controller, which is excellent inside one process and **cannot be adjusted from
outside it**. Setting it explicitly is what makes concurrency a knob Steward can
retune on a live worker rather than a number it can only observe. If you do set
it, Steward uses your value; it only supplies a default when you expressed no
preference.

## Reproducibility stays yours

Inspect's task identity hashes a task's *interface* — name, arguments, model,
resolved plan, config, limits — and not its *implementation*. Change a scorer's
logic, a prompt body, or the contents behind a dataset location, and the
identifier is byte-identical. The mechanism for saying "this is a different eval
now" is `task.version`, and it is yours to bump.

Steward does not verify this, deliberately. The ingredients for a checker are
lying around — every log records the git revision, the installed package
versions, and the dataset's location and size — but whether an upgraded package
matters is a question only the person who wrote the eval can answer, and a
warning that fires during an ordinary week of `pip install -U` is a warning
people learn to route around. The provenance is in every log; querying it is
your prerogative rather than Steward's obligation.
